Google Play Store Apps Data¶

This dataset consists of web scraped data of more than 10,000 Google Play Store apps and 60,000 app reviews. apps_data.csv consists of data about the apps such as category, number of installs, and price. review_data.csv holds reviews of the apps, including the text of the review and sentiment scores. You can join the two tables on the App column.

Note: You can access the data via the File menu or in the Context Panel at the top right of the screen next to Report, under Files. The data dictionary and filenames can be found at the bottom of this workbook.

Source: Kaggle

We've added some guiding questions for analyzing this exciting dataset! Feel free to make this workbook yours by adding and removing cells, or editing any of the existing cells.

Objectives¶

  • Categorical Analysis: Which categories have the highest number of positive reviews amongst the 10 most popular categories?
  • Influence of Paid vs Free: Does being a free app influence ratings?
  • Probability Preferences: Are free apps more likely to receive positive reviews than paid apps?

Scenario: Analyze Factors that Increase the Rating an App Will Receive¶

Background: You are working for an app developer. They are in the process of brainstorming a new app. They want to ensure that their next app scores a high review on the app store, as this can lead to the app being featured on the store homepage.

Objective: They would like you analyze what factors increase the rating an app will receive. They would also like to know what impact reviews have on the final score.

You will need to prepare a report that is accessible to a broad audience. It should outline your motivation, steps, findings, and conclusions.

You can query the pre-loaded CSV files using SQL directly. Here’s a sample query, followed by some sample Python code and outputs:

Data Dictionary¶

data_apps.csv

variable class description
App character The application name
Category character The category the app belongs to
Rating numeric Overall user rating of the app
Reviews numeric Number of user reviews for the app
Size character The size of the app
Installs character Number of user installs for the app
Type character Either "Paid" or "Free"
Price character Price of the app
Content Rating character The age group the app is targeted at - "Children" / "Mature 21+" / "Adult"
Genres character Possibly multiple genres the app belongs to
Last Updated character The date the app was last updated
Current Ver character The current version of the app
Android Ver character The Android version needed for this app

data_reviews.csv

variable class description
App character The application name
Translated_Review character User review (translated to English)
Sentiment character The sentiment of the user - Positive/Negative/Neutral
Sentiment_Polarity character The sentiment polarity score
Sentiment_Subjectivity character The sentiment subjectivity score

For the apps_data dataset, the null rows seem to be related to apps with no rating, which could be related due to the lack of reviews, or a small amount of reviews. We then can draw the following hypothesis:

Hypothesis: Most apps with null ratings will have zero reviews.

Now we check if this hypothesis is actually backed up, or if there is some underlying conclusion we may draw from the data.

In [8]:
-- Calculate the percentage of apps that have null Rating and zero Reviews over the total of Apps with null Rating.

SELECT
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE Rating IS NULL) AS apps_with_no_rating,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE Rating IS NULL AND (TRY_CAST(Reviews AS INTEGER) = 0 OR Reviews IS NULL)
    ) AS apps_with_no_rating_or_review,
    100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE Rating IS NULL AND (TRY_CAST(Reviews AS INTEGER) = 0 OR Reviews IS NULL)) 
    / NULLIF(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE Rating IS NULL),0) AS percentage_of_total
FROM "apps_data"

  • Most of the apps in the sample have a number of Installs that is less than 1,000,000 installs.

  • We notice that most apps with NULL Ratings and nonzero Reviews don't seem to be that popular.
  • For our analysis, we want to consider apps that are somewhat popular apps amongst users. Thus, we will consider apps with non-null Ratings and a nonzero number of Reviews.
  • We proceed to dropping these rows (corresponding to 1474 entries) of apps with no Ratings.
  • The goal here is to work with apps that are somewhat popular, having Ratings and Reviews.

We now focus our attention on looking at how the data is distributed, more specifically:

  • What is the distribution of Rating across apps?
  • What is the distribution of number of Reviews across apps?

Hypothesis:

  1. Most apps will have a higher rating, from 4.0-5.0, with fewer low-rated apps.
  2. The distribution for reviews will be highly-skewed, with fewer apps having a lot of reviews.

2. Data Cleaning¶

Once we have identified our first hypotheses and understood more about the data, it's time to narrow down our analysis to what's really important in order to draw conclusions about app ratings. We then proceed to:

  • Drop rows with NULL ratings
  • Convert Reviews to numeric
  • Since we are not interested in apps with NULL Reviews (therefore NULL Sentiment), we will also drop the rows missing values in our reviews_data.csv dataset
In [15]:
# Drop rows with NULL ratings
# We also notice that there are some Apps with duplicate names, so we will drop those as well
apps_data_clean= apps_data.dropna(subset=['Rating']).drop_duplicates(subset=['App'])

# Convert Reviews to numeric (coerce errors to NaN, then fill with 0 if desired)
apps_data_clean['Reviews'] = pd.to_numeric(apps_data_clean['Reviews'], errors='coerce').fillna(0).astype(int)

apps_data_clean.reset_index(drop=True, inplace=True)

3. Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Now we can begin answering the questions posed as objectives, narrowing our analysis down to actual business questions such as the ones mentioned earlier, we will attack them individually:

(A) Which categories have the highest number of positive reviews amongst the 10 most popular categories?

(B) Does being a free app influence ratings?

(C) Are free apps more likely to receive positive reviews than paid apps?

Before tackling each question individually, we want to examine the correlation between Ratings and the number of Reviews an app has. To assess whether popularity (measured by the number of reviews) is associated with higher ratings, we computed the Pearson correlation between the log‑transformed review count and the app rating.

In [17]:
# We begin by grouping the reviews_data_clean dataset by count of positive reviews, negative reviews and neutral reviews

def count_sentiments(group):
    return pd.Series(
        {
            'count_of_positive_reviews': (group['Sentiment'] == 'Positive').sum(),
            'count_of_negative_reviews': (group['Sentiment'] == 'Negative').sum(),
            'count_of_neutral_reviews': (group['Sentiment'] == 'Neutral').sum()
        })

reviews_data_counts = reviews_data_clean.groupby('App').apply(count_sentiments).reset_index()

# Now we merge the two datasets, reviews_data_counts and apps_data_clean
# In order to grab characteristics of apps such as Type, Installs, Category, etc

df_join = pd.merge(reviews_data_counts, apps_data_clean, on='App', how='left')

df_join.head()

from scipy.stats import pearsonr, shapiro

# First we load the plot data, dropping any missing values rows just to ensure the data is clean
plot_data = df_join.dropna(subset=['Rating', 'Reviews'])

# Compute correlation coefficient (Pearson on log-transformed Reviews)
# Because Reviews is skewed, log-transform for a meaningful correlation
log_reviews = np.log10(plot_data['Reviews'].clip(lower=1))  # safe log
corr, p_value = pearsonr(log_reviews, plot_data['Rating'])

# Create the scatterplot with regression line
ax = sns.regplot(
    data=plot_data,
    x='Reviews',
    y='Rating',
    scatter_kws={'alpha': 0.3, 's': 10},  
    line_kws={'color': 'k', 'lw': 2},
    logx=True,                           
    ci=None)

# Annotate the correlation coefficient on the plot
ax.text(
    0.05, 0.95,                     
    f'Pearson r = {corr:.3f}\np = {p_value:.3e}',
    transform=ax.transAxes,
    verticalalignment='top',
    bbox=dict(boxstyle='round', facecolor='white', alpha=0.7))

ax.set_xscale('log')
ax.set_xlabel('Number of Reviews (log scale)')
ax.set_ylabel('App Rating')
ax.set_title('Rating vs. Number of Reviews')

plt.show()

The result was a statistically significant but weak positive correlation (r = 0.303, p < 0.001).

This means that while apps with more reviews tend to have slightly higher ratings on average, the relationship is far from strong. In practical terms, this means that about 9% of the variation in app ratings can be explained by the number of reviews alone (we use the coefficient of determination, r², to infer that), suggesting that the remaining 91% is driven by other factors, such as app quality, category, pricing model, and user expectations.

Insight: Chasing popularity (i.e., getting more downloads and reviews) alone will not guarantee a high rating. Instead, the focus should be on delivering a quality experience that resonates with users, regardless of whether the app goes viral.

Now let's tackle our first main question:

(A) Which categories have the highest number of positive reviews amongst the 10 most popular categories?¶

In [19]:
# Let's first define what we mean by "most popular categories"
# When talking about most popular categories, we will always  refer to categories with the most installs
# Therefore, we perform this treatment to the data, adding the column Installs_clean

df_join['Installs_clean'] = df_join['Installs'].str.replace('[+,]', '', regex=True).astype(float)
popular_categories = df_join.groupby('Category')['Installs_clean'].sum().sort_values(ascending=False).head(10).index

df_join['total_reviews'] = df_join['count_of_positive_reviews'] +  df_join['count_of_negative_reviews'] + df_join['count_of_neutral_reviews'] 

# Now we aggregate by top categories
top_categories = df_join[['Category',
                          'total_reviews',
                          'count_of_positive_reviews', 
                          'count_of_negative_reviews',
                          'count_of_neutral_reviews']
                        ].groupby('Category').sum().sort_values(by='total_reviews',ascending=False)

# And finally filter using popular_categories
top_categories['positive_over_total'] = 100.0*top_categories['count_of_positive_reviews'] / top_categories['total_reviews']
top_categories_filtered = top_categories.loc[popular_categories].sort_values('count_of_positive_reviews', ascending=False)
top_categories_filtered

Among the 10 most popular categories (by total installs), GAME received by far the highest volume of positive reviews (~3,900), but that's mostly a story of scale — with 6,678 total reviews (more than 3x the next category), even a middling 58.9% positive share adds up to a large raw number. PERSONALIZATION, on the other hand, has the highest ratio of positive to total reviews (70.0%) despite a comparatively modest review volume (1,003) — its users are disproportionately satisfied. PRODUCTIVITY (67.7%) and PHOTOGRAPHY (66.4%) also stand out on this measure. At the other end, SOCIAL has both the smallest review volume (741) and the lowest positive ratio (54.5%) among the top 10, suggesting weaker overall reception.

This suggests that while GAME wins on visibility, developers optimizing for a genuinely satisfied audience — rather than sheer download numbers — may be better served looking at categories like Personalization, Productivity, or Photography, where enthusiasm, not just volume, drives the positive-review share.

(B) Does being a free app influence ratings?¶

We want to tackle this question in a few different ways, to make sure our analysis is fully complete. First, let's outline our core question, "is there a statistically significant difference in average ratings between free and paid apps?". Then we proceed with the following steps:

  • Visualize the distribution of Ratings of apps by Type (Free vs Paid), to get an intuitive feeling of how our apps are distributed and potential outliers
  • Get summary statistics, such as mean, median and standard deviation to quantify the difference
  • Test some assumptions, check if ratings in each group are approximately normal and then decide on which test to use (either a T-Test or Mann-Whitney U test)
  • Compute the difference, how big is the difference in Ratings, pratically speaking?
  • Check confounding variables by comparing the distribution of Reviews between paid and free apps

We normalize the histogram using common_norm=False because of the wild difference in number of Free apps vs Paid apps of 7592 and 604 apps. With common_norm=True, this difference wouldn't be nearly as visible.

Looking at the histogram, we see that the ratings are highly skewed towards the left (pilled at 4.0-4.6) and because of that, a Mann-Whitney U test to check for user preferences is used. But before applying our tests, we will test for the normalty of our data using a Q-Q Plot and a Shapiro-Wilk test.

Basically, what both of these tests will do is:

  • If my data was perfectly shaped, where would each point land?
  • Let's check exactly what shape our data is.
In [28]:
from scipy import stats
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Split the data into two groups
free_ratings = apps_data_clean[apps_data_clean['Type'] == 'Free']['Rating']
paid_ratings = apps_data_clean[apps_data_clean['Type'] == 'Paid']['Rating']

# Create a figure with two subplots side by side
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))

# Q-Q plot for Free apps
stats.probplot(free_ratings, dist="norm", plot=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title('Q-Q Plot: Free Apps')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Theoretical Quantiles')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Sample Quantiles')

# Q-Q plot for Paid apps
stats.probplot(paid_ratings, dist="norm", plot=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title('Q-Q Plot: Paid Apps')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Theoretical Quantiles')
axes[1].set_ylabel('Sample Quantiles')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The Q-Q Plot for Free and Paid apps show exactly what we were expecting, since the points don't exactly hug the line, curving at the left end and flattening at the right end, this is telling that our data is very left-skewed, as we'd expect.

In [29]:
from scipy.stats import shapiro

stat_free, p_free = shapiro(free_ratings)
stat_paid, p_paid = shapiro(paid_ratings)

print(f"Free apps:  W = {stat_free:.4f},  p-value = {p_free:.4e}")
print(f"Paid apps:  W = {stat_paid:.4f},  p-value = {p_paid:.4e}")

Free apps:  W = 0.8750,  p-value = 3.8069e-61
Paid apps:  W = 0.8418,  p-value = 4.7152e-24

This is the nail in the coffin, with a p-value way smaller than 0.05 (since we are testing if the data is normal, having a smaller p-value is not what we'd want), this is strongly suggesting that our data is not normally distributed. Therefore, I will proceed to using the Mann-Whitney test.

First, we define our null hypothesis and alternative hypothesis

  • Null hypothesis: Free and Paid apps have the same rating distribution. Any observed difference is random noise.
  • Alternative hypothesis: There is a meaningful distribution rating distributions differ meaningfully.
In [30]:
from scipy.stats import mannwhitneyu

# Run the Mann-Whitney U test
u_stat, p_value = mannwhitneyu(free_ratings, paid_ratings, alternative='two-sided')

print(f"Mann-Whitney U statistic: {u_stat:.0f}")
print(f"p-value: {p_value:.4e}")

Mann-Whitney U statistic: 1934248
p-value: 1.3054e-10

Here we find our p-value < 0.05, so we reject the null hypothesis, meaning that there is a statistically significant difference between Free and Paid ratings. But is it pratically important? Let's quantify how large this difference actually is using two effect size measures. We use two approaches:

  • Rank-Biserial correlation (r_rb): A correlation coefficient that measures the strength and direction of the difference between two groups when you've used the Mann-Whitney U test. It ranges from -1 to +1.
  • Common Language Effect Size (CLES): The probability that a randomly selected app from one group has a higher rating than a randomly selected app from the other group. It's often more intuitive for non-technical audiences.
In [31]:
# Computing the Rank-Biserial correlation

r_rb = 1 - (2 * u_stat) / (len(free_ratings)*len(paid_ratings))
print(f"Rank-Biserial coefficient: {r_rb:.2f}") 

Rank-Biserial coefficient: 0.16
In [32]:
# Computing the CLES 

cles_free = u_stat / (len(free_ratings)*len(paid_ratings))
cles_paid = 1 - cles_free
print(f"CLES (Free > Paid): {cles_free*100.0:.1f}%")
print(f"CLES (Paid > Free): {cles_paid*100.0:.1f}%")

CLES (Free > Paid): 42.2%
CLES (Paid > Free): 57.8%

The rank-biserial correlation is 0.16, which is a small effect by Cohen's benchmarks, even though the positive direction of the coefficiente tells us that paid apps tend to rank higher. The CLES tells us there's a 58% probability that a randomly selected paid app has a higher rating than a randomly selected free app, only 8 percentage points above chance. In practical terms, the difference in ratings (~0.09 points on a 5-point scale) is unlikely to be noticed by users

Practically speaking, while the difference is statistically significant, it's small enough that 'paid vs free' is not a strong predictor of app ratings. Developers shouldn't assume that charging for their app will meaningfully improve how users rate it.

In [33]:
from scipy.stats import ttest_ind

# We also run the T-test for good measure
t_stat, p_ttest = ttest_ind(free_ratings, paid_ratings, equal_var=False)

print(f"Welch's t-test statistic: {t_stat:.4f}")
print(f"Welch's t-test p-value: {p_ttest:.4e}")

Welch's t-test statistic: -3.9513
Welch's t-test p-value: 8.5690e-05

Insight: Because the data is not normally distributed, my first check comes from the Mann-Whitney U Test, and I decided to use the T-Test as a second check, for good measure. I concluded that there is a statistically significant difference between Free and Paid app ratings. However, the magnitude of the difference (approximately 0.09 points on a 1–5 scale) is very small in practical terms. The next step is to compute the effect size to quantify how meaningful this difference really is.

Confounding Check: Do Paid Apps Have Fewer Reviews?¶

Before concluding that 'being paid' leads to higher ratings, we should check whether paid apps differ systematically in another dimension: the number of reviews they receive. Apps with fewer reviews tend to have more volatile ratings. If paid apps have far fewer reviews, their higher mean rating might be an artifact of small-sample volatility rather than genuine quality.

The statistically significant rating advantage for paid apps (~0.09 points, r_rb ≈ 0.16, small effect) should be interpreted with caution. Because paid apps have an 18x smaller review base, their higher mean rating is partly confounded with review volume and user self-selection. We cannot cleanly isolate "being paid" as the driver of higher ratings; some portion of the observed difference is likely attributable to the fact that paid apps are rated by fewer, more invested users.

Practical takeaway: Pricing model is a weak and confounded predictor of app rating. Developers should not expect that charging for an app will meaningfully improve how users rate it.

Final insight for (B): Paid apps have a statistically significant but small rating advantage (~0.09 points, r_rb = 0.16). A confounding check revealed that paid apps tend to have fewer reviews, which does not fully explain the difference. In practical terms, pricing model alone is a weak predictor of app ratings.

(C) Are free apps more likely to receive positive reviews than paid apps?¶

We approach this question the same way we approached (B), but here the focus is on review-level sentiment (Positive/Negative/Neutral) rather than the star Rating. Since reviews_data_clean only covers apps that have at least one written review, we first need to check how well Free vs. Paid apps are actually represented in this joined dataset before comparing them. Then we:

  • Check the diagnostic: how many Free vs. Paid apps (and reviews) actually make it into this analysis
  • Compare aggregate positive-review rates between Free and Paid apps
  • Check the full sentiment mix (Positive/Negative/Neutral), not just the positive share
  • Move to the app level, not just the review level, reviews from the same app are not independent of each other
  • Run a formal test (chi-square / two-proportion z-test) and, critically, an effect size, to check whether a statistically significant result is also a practically meaningful one
  • Check category composition as a possible confound, the same way we checked review volume as a confound in (B)
In [36]:

Moving from the review level to the app level changes the picture in an important way. Restricting to apps with at least 10 reviews (to avoid single-review noise) leaves 718 Free apps and just 8 Paid apps. The mean per-app positive ratio is still higher for Paid (76.4% vs. 64.6%), so the direction holds, but with only 8 independent Paid data points, this isn't enough to run a reliable statistical test at the app level.

This distinction matters. The tests below treat all 416 Paid reviews as separate pieces of evidence, when they really only reflect 9 independent apps. That's a classic problem, reviews written about the same app are correlated with each other (a genuinely good app tends to generate mostly positive reviews; a mediocre one won't), so they shouldn't be counted as 416 independent observations. We'll still run the formal test for completeness, but we'll read the result with this firmly in mind.

With the descriptive picture in hand, let's put a number on how strong this relationship actually is.

In [42]:
from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency

# Build the 2x2 contingency table
free_row = df_c[df_c['Type'] == 'Free'][['count_of_positive_reviews', 'total_reviews']].sum()
paid_row = df_c[df_c['Type'] == 'Paid'][['count_of_positive_reviews', 'total_reviews']].sum()

table = pd.DataFrame({
    'Positive':     [free_row['count_of_positive_reviews'], paid_row['count_of_positive_reviews']],
    'Non-positive': [free_row['total_reviews'] - free_row['count_of_positive_reviews'],
                     paid_row['total_reviews'] - paid_row['count_of_positive_reviews']]
}, index=['Free', 'Paid'])

# Expected counts under independence
chi2, p, dof, expected = chi2_contingency(table)

print("Observed counts:")
print(table)
print("\nExpected counts under H0:")
print(pd.DataFrame(expected, index=table.index, columns=table.columns).round(2))
print(f"\nMinimum expected count: {expected.min():.2f}  (should be >= 5 for chi-square)")

Observed counts:
      Positive  Non-positive
Free     22748         12765
Paid       325            91

Expected counts under H0:
      Positive  Non-positive
Free  22805.85      12707.15
Paid    267.15        148.85

Minimum expected count: 148.85  (should be >= 5 for chi-square)
In [43]:
chi2, p, dof, expected = chi2_contingency(table)

print(f"Chi-square statistic: {chi2:.2f}")
print(f"Degrees of freedom:   {dof}")
print(f"p-value:              {p:.4e}")
print(f"Total reviews (N):    {table.values.sum():,}")

Chi-square statistic: 34.81
Degrees of freedom:   1
p-value:              3.6298e-09
Total reviews (N):    35,929

The chi-square test returns χ² = 34.81 (df = 1, p ≈ 3.63 × 10⁻⁹), which on its own would normally read as strong evidence that Type and review sentiment are related. But per the caveat above, this test assumes each of the 35,929 reviews is an independent observation. In reality they cluster into 816 apps, with only 9 of them Paid, so this p-value is almost certainly overstating how confident we should be. A more honest read: within this specific, tiny sample of 9 Paid apps, the positive rate is meaningfully higher than in the Free sample, but we can't yet say that generalizes to "Paid apps" as a category.

In [44]:
import numpy as np

p_free = table.loc['Free', 'Positive'] / table.loc['Free'].sum()
p_paid = table.loc['Paid', 'Positive'] / table.loc['Paid'].sum()

n_free = table.loc['Free'].sum()
n_paid = table.loc['Paid'].sum()

p_pool = (table.loc['Free', 'Positive'] + table.loc['Paid', 'Positive']) / (n_free + n_paid)
se = np.sqrt(p_pool * (1 - p_pool) * (1/n_free + 1/n_paid))
z = (p_free - p_paid) / se

from scipy.stats import norm
p_two_sided = 2 * (1 - norm.cdf(abs(z)))

print(f"Free positive proportion: {p_free:.4f}")
print(f"Paid positive proportion: {p_paid:.4f}")
print(f"Difference (Free - Paid): {p_free - p_paid:+.4f}")
print(f"z-statistic:              {z:.4f}")
print(f"Two-sided p-value:        {p_two_sided:.4e}")

Free positive proportion: 0.6406
Paid positive proportion: 0.7812
Difference (Free - Paid): -0.1407
z-statistic:              -5.9517
Two-sided p-value:        2.6541e-09

The two-proportion z-test (z = -5.95, p ≈ 2.65 × 10⁻⁹) is mathematically equivalent to the chi-square test above so agreement here isn't independent confirmation.

In [45]:
n = table.values.sum()
phi = np.sqrt(chi2 / n)

print(f"Cramér's V (phi): {phi:.4f}")
print("Benchmarks: 0.10 = small, 0.30 = medium, 0.50 = large")

Cramér's V (phi): 0.0311
Benchmarks: 0.10 = small, 0.30 = medium, 0.50 = large

Now this is more useful, Cramér's V = 0.031 is far below even the "small effect" threshold of 0.10. In other words, even setting the sample-size concerns aside, the statistical relationship between Type and sentiment is very negligible. The tiny p-values above come from having tens of thousands of reviews, not from the relationship being strong, with a large enough N, even a trivial difference becomes "statistically significant". This is the same lesson from (B): statistical significance and practical importance are two different questions, and here the practical importance is close to zero.

The category breakdown explains why this sample can't be treated as representative: the 9 Paid apps fall into only 5 categories, those being; GAME (2 apps), FAMILY (1), MEDICAL (2), PERSONALIZATION (3), SPORTS (1), compared to Free apps which are spread across roughly 30 categories. Notably, PERSONALIZATION, which had the highest positive-review ratio of any category back in (A) (≈70%), makes up a third of this entire Paid sample (3 of 9 apps). If Personalization apps are simply well-reviewed regardless of price, that alone could explain the Paid group's higher positive rate. "Being paid" shouldn't be treated as a cause at all. Since we don't have enough Paid apps here to separate a category effect from a pricing effect.

Final insight for (C): Read naively, the review-level numbers suggest Paid apps receive positive reviews at a higher rate than Free apps (78.1% vs. 64.1%, p < 0.001), the opposite of what the original question assumes. But three checks undercut that reading:

  1. The effect size is negligible (Cramér's V = 0.031).
  2. The review-level tests overstate confidence, since they treat 416 correlated reviews from just 9 apps as if they were 416 independent data points.
  3. Those 9 apps are concentrated in a handful of categories. So category, not pricing, may be doing the real work.

Practical takeaway: With the data available, there isn't reliable evidence that Free apps are more (or less) likely to receive positive reviews than Paid apps. The apparent gap is more plausibly an artifact of a very small, non-representative sample of Paid apps than a genuine effect of price, which is consistent with the finding in (B) that pricing model is, at best, a weak and unreliable predictor of how users respond to an app.

4. Conclusions & Recommendations¶

Summary of Findings¶

Question Answer Confidence
(A) Which categories get the most positive reviews? GAME leads in raw positive-review volume (~3,900). Which is due to a function of scale, not sentiment quality (58.9% positive, near the bottom of the top 10). PERSONALIZATION (70.0%), PRODUCTIVITY (67.7%), and PHOTOGRAPHY (66.4%) have the highest share of positive reviews among the top 10 installed categories. High, based on the full review dataset
(B) Does Free vs. Paid influence star Rating? Paid apps rate marginally higher (4.26 vs. 4.17, ~0.09 pts), statistically significant (Mann-Whitney p < 0.001) but a small effect (r_rb = 0.16), and confounded by Paid apps having far fewer reviews. Moderate. Real, but small and confounded
(C) Are Free apps more likely to get positive reviews than Paid? No reliable evidence either way. Raw numbers favor Paid, but the effect size is negligible and the Paid sample (9 apps) is too small and non-representative to trust. Low, sample too small to conclude

Answering the Business Question¶

Going back to the original goal what factors increase the rating an app will receive, pricing model (Free vs. Paid) is not the lever to pull. Across both (B) and (C), any "Paid apps do better" signal we found was small, statistically fragile, or explainable by confounds like review volume or category mix rather than price itself.

What the analysis does support:

  • Category matters more than pricing. PERSONALIZATION, PRODUCTIVITY, and PHOTOGRAPHY show the strongest audience sentiment among popular categories, while SOCIAL lags behind on both volume and positivity.
  • Review volume and rating are only weakly related (r ≈ 0.30, r² ≈ 9%), so chasing installs or reviews alone won't guarantee a better rating. The remaining ~91% comes down to the product itself.
  • Sample sizes vary a lot by segment (e.g., 9 Paid apps with reviews vs. 807 Free), so any pricing decision shouldn't be based on this dataset's Paid-app numbers.

Recommendations¶

  1. When choosing a category for the new app, prioritize categories with historically strong sentiment (Personalization, Productivity, Photography) over pure install volume.
  2. Don't treat "Free vs. Paid" as a rating-optimization lever.
  3. Invest directly in whatever drives product quality and user experience, since that accounts for the large majority of rating variance not explained by review count.
  4. Collect more Paid-app review data over time before drawing firm conclusions about pricing and sentiment, 9 apps is not enough to generalize from.

Limitations¶

  • The Paid-app sample used for sentiment analysis in (C) is extremely small (9 apps), limiting how far its conclusions can be trusted.
  • Reviews are user-submitted and self-selected. Notice that users with strongly positive or negative experiences are more likely to leave a review than moderately satisfied ones, which can bias sentiment in either direction.
  • Sentiment is a translated, coarse Positive/Negative/Neutral label rather than the raw review text, so nuance within reviews is lost.
  • The dataset is a single scrape in time and doesn't capture how ratings evolve after an app updates.
